title: Muffin — Data coverage
description: How complete the data is and where the gaps are. From market.coverage_sample, a twice-daily snapshot of market.coverage_current — one definition, so the table can never disagree with the view.

panels.title: Funnel — the stages that genuinely gate each other
panels.description:
A REAL FUNNEL, over the five stages that are genuinely nested — each one REQUIRES the stage above it. Sector and industry are read off the profile response, and the profile needs a symbol, so the chain is causal rather than merely sorted.

The other facets are NOT in here on purpose. Measured 2026-08-28, `metrics` (8,948) EXCEEDS `statements` (8,842), because metrics also come straight from SEC XBRL rather than only from stored statements — so putting them in a funnel would assert a pipeline that does not exist. They are in the bar panel below, which claims no ordering.

Grafana OSS has no funnel panel; a horizontal bar gauge sorted descending is the honest equivalent and needs no plugin.

DELIBERATELY EXCLUDES the four SEC-sourced facets. This funnel is about stages that GATE one another — no symbol means no price, no price means no performance — and segments gate nothing and are gated by nothing in it: a company with no CIK simply has no source, which is an absence rather than a blocked stage. Putting them here would make the funnel's last bar look like the pipeline's bottleneck when it is a property of the universe. They are on the 'Independent facets' bargauge beside it.

targets.rawSql:
select 'universe' as metric, sum(securities)::float as value   from market.coverage_sample
 where dimension = 'country_sector'
   and sampled_at = (select max(sampled_at) from market.coverage_sample)
   and security_type_code = 'equity'
   and split_part(bucket,'|',1) like '$country'
   and split_part(bucket,'|',2) like '$sector'

panels.title: Independent facets — coverage, no dependency implied
panels.description:
Every facet that is NOT part of the nested chain, sorted by coverage. Deliberately a bar chart rather than a funnel: these do not gate one another, and ordering them would invent a pipeline. Scoped by the Country and Sector variables above.

The four SEC-sourced facets belong HERE and not in the funnel: they gate nothing and nothing gates them. They are shown as a percentage of `sec_filers`, because that is the only population that can have them.

panels.title: Every facet for this scope — have, missing, percent
panels.description:
The 'what exactly is missing for CN energy' view. One row per facet for whatever the Country and Sector variables select: All/All is the whole universe, US/All a country, All/energy a sector, US/energy the cross. `missing` is the actionable number — it is the count of securities a resource still has to reach.

THE LAST FOUR ROWS ARE MEASURED AGAINST `sec_filers`, NOT `securities`. Segments, geography, SIC and the weighted classification come from SEC filings and nowhere else, so 8,834 of 12,350 equities can never have them — dividing by the whole bucket would measure how many of its companies file with SEC, not how well covered they are, and beside `symbol` at 97% it reads as a catastrophic gap. They are listed here rather than only on the business-lines row because this panel says EVERY facet, and a panel that claims completeness while dropping four is read as complete.

panels.title: Country × sector — completeness (sortable; worst first by default)
panels.description:
Every (country, sector) bucket holding at least 20 securities — 106 of the 637 combinations. Click a column to re-sort; the default is worst-first because that is where the work is.

IT USED TO BE `limit 60`, AND THAT HID THE UNITED STATES. US is the best-covered country, so its eleven real sectors ranked 90-98 of 106 and fell off the end — leaving only `US / unknown` (92 securities with no sector, genuinely 0%) visible, which read as 'the US is missing'. A worst-first list truncated at an arbitrary row silently deletes whatever is healthy, and the healthy things are the ones you check when something looks wrong.

The >=20 floor stays: a completeness figure over a handful of securities is noise, and a two-stock bucket at 0% would otherwise top the list for ever.

THE SIZE FLOOR IS A VARIABLE, NOT A CONSTANT. At the default of 20 it hides 531 of 637 buckets — a defensible choice (a 2-security bucket at 0% is noise, not a signal) but not one that should be invisible. Set `Min securities in bucket` to 1 to see all of them. The panel previously ALSO carried `limit 60`, which deleted the United States: 106 buckets cleared the floor, the US ranked 90-98 of them BECAUSE it is well covered, and the only US row that survived was `US / unknown` at 0%.

Every percentage column is coloured by a NEGATIVE match. It used to name `complete %` alone, so `statements %` and `industry %` rendered as plain numbers in a heatmap — found by CI, not by looking, and the same stale-enumeration shape as the four facets that rendered uncoloured on the × facet tables.

**`core %` is the typed GATE** — holds every facet `required_facet` demands of its type — and **`all facets %` is BREADTH**: of the 23 facets a security could have, how many it has, with the four regulator-sourced ones excluded from the denominator where no regulator can serve it. One number was ambiguous: a bucket can read 100% core while not one of its companies has a business line.

targets.rawSql:
select split_part(bucket,'|',1) as "country",
       split_part(bucket,'|',2) as "sector",
       securities,
       round(100.0*complete/nullif(securities,0),1) as "core %", round(100.0*present_facets/nullif(applicable_facets,0),1) as "all facets %",
       round(100.0*with_statements/nullif(securities,0),1) as "statements %",
       round(100.0*with_industry/nullif(securities,0),1)   as "industry %"
  from market.coverage_sample
 where dimension = 'country_sector'
   and sampled_at = (select max(sampled_at) from market.coverage_sample)
   and security_type_code = 'equity'
   and securities >= $minsize

panels.description:
One row per country, one column per facet, filtered to equities. Countries below the `$minsize` floor are hidden — set it to 1 to see all 164.

Every cell is the percent of that group's equities carrying the facet, so a column reads as a pipeline stage and a row reads as a group's overall health. Sort by any column to ask 'who is worst at statements'. NO ROW LIMIT — a worst-first list truncated at an arbitrary row silently deletes whatever is healthy, which is how `limit 60` hid the United States.

THE LAST FOUR COLUMNS ARE MEASURED AGAINST `sec_filers`, NOT `securities`. Segments, geography, SIC and the weighted classification come from SEC filings and nowhere else, so 8,834 of 12,350 equities can never have them — dividing by the whole bucket would measure how many of a country's companies file with SEC rather than how well covered they are. They are listed here because this panel enumerates every facet, and one that drops four while claiming completeness is read as complete.

TWO COMPLETENESS NUMBERS, because one was ambiguous. **`core %`** is the typed GATE — does this hold every facet `required_facet` demands of its type — and is exactly the number previously labelled `complete %`. **`all facets %`** is breadth: of the 23 facets a security COULD have, how many it has. The colouring matcher is a NEGATIVE match, not a list of facet names. panels.title: Business lines, filings and classification — SEC-sourced, so read them against the SEC-filer population
The denominator — what each population can even have
panels.description:
READ THIS FIRST. Everything in this row comes from SEC filings and nowhere else: measured 2026-08-29, ESEF block-tags its IFRS 8 segment notes as text and EDINET carries zero segment axes, so a company with no CIK has no source at all.

That is why `segments` is NOT in `market.required_facet`. Requiring it of every equity would report ~71% of the universe permanently broken against data that is correct — the same miscalibration that made ETFs read 0% complete because `price` was required of a type this pipeline has never stored bars for. A structurally unreachable completeness number gets ignored within a week, and the real regressions go with it.

So the split is a DIMENSION. `sec_filer = yes` is the honest denominator for the four facets below; `no` should read near zero and its being near zero is not a defect.

targets.rawSql:
select
  case bucket when 'yes' then 'SEC filer (has a CIK)' else 'no CIK — no segment source exists' end as population,
  securities,
  round(100.0*with_segments/nullif(securities,0),1)           as segments_pct,
  round(100.0*with_segment_geography/nullif(securities,0),1)  as geography_pct,
  round(100.0*with_sic/nullif(securities,0),1)                as sic_pct,
  round(100.0*with_weighted_industry/nullif(securities,0),1)  as weighted_industry_pct
from market.coverage_sample
where dimension = 'segment_source'
  and security_type_code = 'equity'
  and sampled_at = (select max(sampled_at) from market.coverage_sample)
order by bucket

panels.title: Business lines — coverage of the SEC-filer population
panels.description:
The four SEC-sourced facets, measured against the population that can have them (`sec_filer = yes`).

`segments` is a company with a READABLE business-line breakdown — a partition-1 annual row in `security_segment_spine`, not merely a parsed filing. `geography` is where it earns, resolved without curation from the published ISO and region members. `weighted_industry` is the one that answers the original question: a company whose single sector label is known to be misleading, and by how much.

SAMPLED TWICE A DAY, so `showPoints: always` — a timeseries draws a LINE, and two points in a 30-day window is indistinguishable from no data. That cost a round of "why is this empty" on the coverage dashboard once already.

targets.rawSql:
select sampled_at as time, m as metric, v as value from (
  select sampled_at,
         'business lines'      as m, round(100.0*with_segments/nullif(securities,0),1) as v
    from market.coverage_sample
   where dimension='segment_source' and bucket='sec' and security_type_code='equity'
  union all
  select sampled_at, 'geography', round(100.0*with_segment_geography/nullif(securities,0),1)
    from market.coverage_sample
   where dimension='segment_source' and bucket='sec' and security_type_code='equity'
  union all
  select sampled_at, 'SIC code', round(100.0*with_sic/nullif(securities,0),1)
    from market.coverage_sample
   where dimension='segment_source' and bucket='sec' and security_type_code='equity'
  union all
  select sampled_at, 'weighted industry', round(100.0*with_weighted_industry/nullif(securities,0),1)
    from market.coverage_sample
   where dimension='segment_source' and bucket='sec' and security_type_code='equity'
) s where $__timeFilter(sampled_at) order by sampled_at

panels.title: Which countries have business lines, and which never will
panels.description:
Segment coverage per country. A country reading 0% is usually not a backlog — it is a country whose companies do not file with SEC, and the only ones that do are those with a US listing filing a 20-F or 40-F (787 non-US securities: ASML, SAP, Diageo, Infosys, MUFG, TSMC, Novo, Toyota).

The floor is the reader-controlled `$minsize` variable, selectable down to 1, so nothing is hidden by a decision the reader cannot see — a hardcoded `limit` over a worst-first sort once made the United States, the best-covered country in the universe, appear as the worst.

targets.rawSql:
select
  bucket as country,
  securities,
  with_segments as with_business_lines,
  round(100.0*with_segments/nullif(securities,0),1) as segments_pct,
  round(100.0*with_segment_geography/nullif(securities,0),1) as geography_pct
from market.coverage_sample
where dimension = 'country'
  and security_type_code = 'equity'
  and sampled_at = (select max(sampled_at) from market.coverage_sample)
  and securities >= $minsize
order by round(100.0*with_segments/nullif(securities,0),1) desc nulls last, securities desc

panels.title: Which sectors have business lines
panels.description:
The same question by sector. A conglomerate-heavy sector should be the one where a single label is least informative, so low coverage here is where the feature is worth the most rather than where it matters least.

`weighted_industry` is the column that pays off: it counts companies whose revenue and profit splits DISAGREE about what they are — Amazon reads 62% consumer-discretionary by revenue and 57% information-technology by profit.

targets.rawSql:
select
  bucket as sector,
  securities,
  with_segments as with_business_lines,
  round(100.0*with_segments/nullif(securities,0),1) as segments_pct,
  with_weighted_industry as reclassified,
  round(100.0*with_weighted_industry/nullif(securities,0),1) as weighted_industry_pct
from market.coverage_sample
where dimension = 'sector'
  and security_type_code = 'equity'
  and sampled_at = (select max(sampled_at) from market.coverage_sample)
  and securities >= $minsize
order by round(100.0*with_segments/nullif(securities,0),1) desc nulls last, securities desc

list.name: country
list.label: Country
list.query:
select distinct split_part(bucket,'|',1) as __text, split_part(bucket,'|',1) as __value
  from market.coverage_sample
 where dimension='country_sector'
   and sampled_at=(select max(sampled_at) from market.coverage_sample)

list.name: sector
list.label: Sector
list.query:
select distinct split_part(bucket,'|',2) as __text, split_part(bucket,'|',2) as __value
  from market.coverage_sample
 where dimension='country_sector'
   and sampled_at=(select max(sampled_at) from market.coverage_sample)

list.name: minsize
list.label: Min securities in bucket
list.description: Buckets smaller than this are hidden. A 2-security bucket at 0% would otherwise top a worst-first list. Set to 1 to see EVERY bucket — nothing is hidden by a decision you cannot see.
